questions.subtopic: 3B1 Audit universe and engagement sources. A Topical Requirement and the risk ranking
questions.question: Chief audit executive Freja's risk assessment rates a Danish shipper's cyber risk moderate, below the eight planned areas; a director says the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement still demands a cyber engagement. Which reply is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agreed: Topical Requirements are mandatory, so every plan must cover cyber
options.B: Not so: it sets the minimum once assurance work takes in cyber
options.C: Agreed, though advisory work on cyber would also satisfy it
options.D: Not so, provided the board approves a documented exclusion of cyber

questions.key_concept: A Topical Requirement governs engagements that take in its topic; the risk assessment, not the requirement, decides whether the plan includes one.
questions.pre_read: Recall the three cases in which a Topical Requirement applies, and what decides which engagements enter the plan.
questions.correct_explanation: The Cybersecurity Topical Requirement applies when cyber is the subject of a planned engagement, turns up during one, or is requested outside the plan, and then sets a mandatory minimum for assurance work. It sets no risk level that forces an engagement: with cyber rated moderate, Standard 9.4's risk assessment decides the plan. Option A mistakes mandatory conformance inside an engagement for a duty to plan one every year.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: conformance is mandatory once an assurance engagement covers cyber, but the requirement does not put cyber in every plan; the risk assessment decides that.
wrong_explanations.C: For advisory work on the topic, conformance is only recommended, and nothing in the requirement obliges any cyber engagement this year.
wrong_explanations.D: The board approves the plan as a whole, but the requirement creates no plan-level exclusion to approve; exclusions are single requirements inside an engagement, recorded with a reason.

tips: Eliminate: C, because conformance is only recommended for advisory work, and D, because exclusions cover single requirements inside an engagement, with a recorded reason, not board approval.
Final two: B beats A because the requirement is mandatory inside assurance engagements that take in cyber, while the risk assessment decides whether the plan holds one.
Exam cue: on CIA plan questions, a Topical Requirement answers how a topic is audited; the risk assessment answers whether it is audited this period.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Audit universe and engagement sources. A request the reserve can absorb
questions.question: Midyear, a Peruvian bakery chain's chief executive asks chief audit executive Rosa to review a new loyalty app; the plan's reserved hours would cover it without moving planned work. What should Rosa do FIRST?

options.A: Schedule the review in the reserved hours now
options.B: Keep the reserve for contingencies and decline the review
options.C: Seek the board's approval before considering the request further
options.D: Weigh the app's risks and benefit before committing the reserve

questions.key_concept: A request is weighed on its risk, the time it needs and its benefit before reserved hours are committed to it.
questions.pre_read: Recall how Standard 9.4's considerations treat ad hoc requests and the share of hours a plan holds back for them.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.4's considerations tell the chief audit executive to weigh advisory and ad hoc requests by their risk, the time they need and their benefit, and to hold a share of hours for such requests. Rosa first judges whether the app warrants it. Option A spends the reserve because hours are free, but reserved hours go to requests that merit them on risk, time and benefit.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: reserved hours exist for requests like this, but a request earns them on risk, time and benefit; the chief executive's request still has to be weighed.
wrong_explanations.B: The considerations hold the reserve for contingencies and ad hoc requests alike; a request like this is weighed on its risk, time and benefit, not refused by default.
wrong_explanations.C: Board approval covers significant changes, such as postponing work on significant risks; nothing planned moves here, and an unweighed request cannot yet be judged significant.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the reserve serves ad hoc requests as well as contingencies, and C, because board approval is for significant changes, and nothing planned moves here.
Final two: D beats A because reserved hours go to requests that rank on risk, time and benefit; who asked does not decide.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about requests, weigh risk, resources and benefit first; take a change to the board when it displaces significant planned work.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Audit universe and engagement sources. A risk spread across three units
questions.question: Chief audit executive Camilo scores a Colombian retailer's audit universe unit by unit; supplier kickback risk appears in procurement, logistics and store operations, rated moderate in each. How should Camilo BEST treat it?

options.A: Score it in each unit, weighted up for its fraud element
options.B: Plan fraud testing in each of the three units this year
options.C: Evaluate it once across the three units as one risk
options.D: Average the three unit ratings into one overall rating

questions.key_concept: A risk that spans several units, such as fraud, should be evaluated across them; unit-by-unit scores can understate it.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 9.4's considerations say about risks tied to more than one unit or process.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.4's considerations single out risks, fraud and third-party risk among them, that reach across several units: they deserve careful attention and a fuller evaluation than one unit's score gives. Scored separately, a kickback scheme spanning buying, delivery and stores looks moderate everywhere and may never reach the plan. Option A weights each unit's score, but each score still sees only that unit's share.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: weighting each unit's score recognizes the fraud element, but each score still sees one unit's share; a risk tied to several units should be evaluated across them.
wrong_explanations.B: Testing in every unit this year jumps ahead of the ranking; a moderate risk enters the plan by its overall level, not by default.
wrong_explanations.D: Averaging three moderate scores still gives a moderate score; a risk spread across units needs its combined reach evaluated, not arithmetic on the unit scores.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a risk earns engagements through its ranking, not by default, and D, because averaging moderate scores still yields a moderate one, with no look at the combined reach.
Final two: C beats A because weighting each unit's score still sees one unit's share; a risk tied to several units should be evaluated across them.
Exam cue: on CIA audit universe questions, look for fraud, IT, third-party or compliance risks that span units; they are evaluated together.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Building the risk-based audit plan. What must inform the risk assessment
questions.question: Chief audit executive Lars's documented risk assessment for a Swedish utility draws on senior managers' interviews, past engagement results and Lars's grasp of its governance and controls. Which further input is MOST clearly required?

options.A: Senior management's approval of the final risk ranking
options.B: The board's views on strategies, objectives and risks
options.C: The external auditor's assessment of reporting risks
options.D: Management's risk register, once its process is judged effective

questions.key_concept: The plan's risk assessment must be documented, done at least yearly and informed by input from both the board and senior management.
questions.pre_read: Recall the inputs Standard 9.4 requires for the organizationwide risk assessment, and which inputs are only optional.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.4 requires the documented assessment behind the plan to draw on input from the board as well as senior management, together with the chief audit executive's understanding of governance, risk management and control. Lars has senior management's views but not the board's. Management's register may be used once its risk management process is judged effective, a consideration rather than a requirement, so option D is optional where B is required.

wrong_explanations.A: Senior management gives input to the risk assessment; it does not approve the ranking, and the board, not senior management, approves the resulting plan.
wrong_explanations.C: The external auditor is an assurance provider to coordinate with; its view can help, but the Standard does not require it as an input.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a register may be relied on after the chief audit executive concludes risk management is effective, but that is an option, not a required input.

tips: Eliminate: A, because senior management gives input and does not approve, and C, because coordinating with the external auditor does not make its view a required input.
Final two: B beats D because the board's input is a requirement of the risk assessment, while relying on management's register is optional and conditional.
Exam cue: on CIA plan questions, the risk assessment needs input from both the board and senior management; tools and registers are optional.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Building the risk-based audit plan. A high-risk area left without assurance
questions.question: Chief audit executive Kemal's draft plan for a Turkish airline gives its high-risk maintenance-system migration advisory work only, judging advice during design more useful than assurance. Which step is MOST clearly required of Kemal?

options.A: Tell the board and senior management why the migration lacks assurance
options.B: Replace a lower-risk engagement so the migration gets assurance
options.C: Have senior management approve leaving assurance out of the plan
options.D: Record the reason in the documented risk assessment

questions.key_concept: When the plan leaves a high-risk area without an assurance engagement, the chief audit executive must tell the board and senior management why, in time.
questions.pre_read: Recall the four matters Standard 9.4 says the chief audit executive must communicate in time to the board and senior management.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.4 requires the chief audit executive to tell the board and senior management in time why a high-risk area gets no assurance engagement in the plan. Kemal may judge advice during the design the better use of hours; the Standard does not overrule that choice, it requires the reason to be shared. Option B, swapping assurance in, is a choice Kemal could make, not one the Standards impose.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: swapping out lower-risk work is one way to cover the migration, but it is a judgment Kemal may make; the requirement is to explain the gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Senior management gives input to the plan but approves neither the plan nor its gaps; the board approves the plan, and both bodies are told.
wrong_explanations.D: Recording the reason documents the choice, but Standard 9.4 requires the reason to reach the board and senior management in time, not only to sit on file.

tips: Eliminate: C, because senior management does not approve the plan or its gaps, and D, because a reason on file does not tell the board and senior management.
Final two: A beats B because the Standards require the gap to be explained, not filled; covering the migration instead is one choice among several.
Exam cue: on CIA plan questions, a high-risk area left without an assurance engagement is explained, with the reason, to the board and senior management in time.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Building the risk-based audit plan. An urgent change between board meetings
questions.question: A supplier's ransomware attack means chief audit executive Marisol must postpone a Manila hospital's pharmacy engagement for supplier-access work, a significant change; the audit committee next meets in three months. What is Marisol's BEST course?

options.A: Make the change; tell the board and senior management at year end
options.B: Hold the change for the meeting, then seek the board's approval
options.C: Make the change once the chief executive approves it in writing
options.D: Inform the board and senior management now; seek formal approval soon

questions.key_concept: Significant plan changes need board approval; when a risk cannot wait for a meeting, the board should hear at once and approve formally soon after.
questions.pre_read: Recall how Standard 9.4 treats significant interim changes, and what its considerations say when a change cannot wait.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.4 requires significant interim changes to be discussed with the board and senior management and approved by the board. Its considerations add that when risks force a revision before a formal discussion can be held, the board should be informed immediately and approve formally as soon as possible. Option B keeps the approval but leaves the attack's exposure unaudited for three months, against the requirement that the plan be updated in time.

wrong_explanations.A: Year-end reporting skips board approval of a significant change; the board should hear at once and approve formally soon after.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: board approval is right, but waiting three months leaves an urgent risk uncovered; the considerations allow telling the board now and approving formally soon after.
wrong_explanations.C: Senior management gives input on the plan; it cannot approve a significant change, which belongs to the board.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a significant change needs the board's approval, not a year-end mention, and C, because the chief executive cannot approve changes to the plan.
Final two: D beats B because an urgent risk should not wait for the next meeting; the board is told now and gives formal approval as soon as possible.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about urgent plan changes, look for immediate notice to the board followed by formal approval; neither silence nor a long wait.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Coordinating with other assurance providers. A provider who will not coordinate
questions.question: A Czech brewer's quality assurance head has refused, in writing, chief audit executive Tereza's requests to align supplier audits, so suppliers face duplicate visits. Where should Tereza take the concern FIRST?

options.A: To the audit committee at its next meeting
options.B: Into the next internal audit report on quality assurance
options.C: To senior management at its next leadership meeting
options.D: To the quality assurance head once more, at a formal meeting

questions.key_concept: When coordination with another assurance provider fails, the chief audit executive must raise the concern with senior management, and with the board if necessary.
questions.pre_read: Recall the order Standard 9.5 sets for raising concerns when coordination with other providers cannot be achieved.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.5 requires the chief audit executive to coordinate with internal and external assurance providers, so effort is not duplicated and gaps show. When an appropriate level of coordination cannot be achieved, the concern must go to senior management and, if necessary, the board. A written refusal shows coordination has failed with the provider, so Tereza raises it with senior management; the audit committee hears it if that does not resolve it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the board may need to hear it, but Standard 9.5 sends the concern to senior management first and to the board only if necessary.
wrong_explanations.B: A coordination concern is raised with senior management when it arises; holding it for an engagement report delays it and treats a planning issue as a finding.
wrong_explanations.D: Tereza's written requests were the discussion; once they are refused in writing, coordination has failed and the concern goes to senior management.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a coordination concern is raised when it arises, not saved for a report, and D, because a written refusal means coordination has already failed with the provider.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 9.5 sets the order: senior management first, then the board if necessary.
Exam cue: on CIA coordination questions, a provider that will not cooperate is raised with senior management before the board.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Coordinating with other assurance providers. Relying on an engineering firm once
questions.question: For one engagement only, chief audit executive Aliya plans to rely on an engineering firm's dam inspections at a Kazakh utility, having judged the firm's work sound. Which step is MOST clearly required?

options.A: Document the basis for relying on the firm's inspections
options.B: Agree in writing the testing and evidence the firm must supply
options.C: Retest every inspection before using the firm's results
options.D: Disclose the reliance in the engagement's final communication

questions.key_concept: Reliance on another provider requires a documented basis, and the chief audit executive stays responsible for internal audit's conclusions.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 9.5 requires when relying on another provider, and what it suggests for long-term reliance.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.5 requires the chief audit executive to document the basis for relying on another assurance provider, and leaves responsibility for internal audit's conclusions with the chief audit executive. Its considerations add that ongoing or long-term reliance should rest on a documented agreement on the testing and evidence required. Aliya relies once, so option B fits a standing arrangement, while A is required here.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a written agreement on testing and evidence is suggested for ongoing or long-term reliance; for one engagement, the requirement is to document the basis.
wrong_explanations.C: Retesting is the route when the evaluation shows the work cannot be relied on; Aliya judged the firm's work sound.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 11.3 requires disclosing reliance in a conclusion at business-unit or organization level; the requirement here is documenting the basis.

tips: Eliminate: C, because retesting follows a failed evaluation, not a passed one, and D, because disclosing reliance is required in wider conclusions at business-unit or organization level.
Final two: A beats B because documenting the basis is required for any reliance, while a written agreement is suggested for ongoing or long-term reliance.
Exam cue: on CIA reliance questions, evaluate the provider, document the basis and keep responsibility; ongoing reliance adds a written agreement.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Building the risk-based audit plan. Who agrees what a significant change is
questions.question: Writing a protocol for changes to a Moroccan phosphate group's internal audit plan, chief audit executive Youssef must settle who sets the criteria for a significant change. Which arrangement is BEST?

options.A: The board sets them and records them in its minutes
options.B: Youssef, the board and senior management agree them jointly
options.C: Youssef and the board agree them; senior management is informed
options.D: Senior management sets them and reports them to the board

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive, board and senior management should agree what counts as a significant plan change; the board then approves each such change.
questions.pre_read: Recall who Standard 9.4's considerations say should agree the criteria for significant changes to the plan.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.4's considerations say the criteria defining a significant change should be settled jointly by the chief audit executive, the board and senior management, then written into the function's methodologies with the protocol for handling changes. Under the requirement the board approves each significant change, and both bodies discuss interim changes. Option C has senior management told rather than agreeing.

wrong_explanations.A: The board approves each significant change, but setting the criteria by itself leaves out the chief audit executive and senior management, who should agree them.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: joint agreement is right, but the considerations name senior management among the parties who agree the criteria, not one merely told; it also discusses interim changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Senior management gives input and support; it does not set the rules for when the board must approve plan changes.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the board approves changes but does not set the rules by itself, and D, because senior management gives input, not rules.
Final two: B beats C because the considerations make senior management one of the three parties who agree the criteria, not a body that is merely told.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, separate who approves a change from who agrees the rules for changes; the second is shared.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Audit universe and engagement sources. A compliance list of the laws that apply
questions.question: New chief audit executive Dana, preparing a Romanian drug distributor's first risk-based plan, receives the compliance team's list of laws that apply. Which step is MOST clearly required of Dana?

options.A: Study each listed law closely enough to test compliance with it
options.B: Adopt the compliance team's list as the plan's legal input
options.C: Learn how the organization tracks and manages legal compliance
options.D: Plan a compliance engagement for each listed law this cycle

questions.key_concept: To plan, the chief audit executive must understand the processes the organization uses to track and manage its compliance with laws and regulations.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 9.1 requires the chief audit executive to understand before building the strategy and plan.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.1 requires the chief audit executive, before building the strategy and plan, to understand the processes the organization uses to find and handle its key risk areas, legal and regulatory compliance among them. Dana learns the process behind the list: who tracks new laws and how compliance is managed. Standard 9.4's considerations add that management's risk information is relied on only once its processes are judged effective, so the list is not simply adopted.

wrong_explanations.A: Standard 1.3 has internal auditors understand and abide by the laws that apply, but planning needs the organization's process; testing compliance with a law is engagement work.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the list is a useful source, but management's risk information is relied on only after its processes are judged effective, which needs the understanding Standard 9.1 requires.
wrong_explanations.D: A risk-based plan weighs laws in the risk assessment and considers engagements a law requires; it does not give every listed law its own engagement each cycle.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the chief audit executive must understand the organization's processes, not master each law, and D, because a risk-based plan does not give each listed law an engagement every cycle.
Final two: C beats B because adopting management's list first requires knowing how it was built; Standard 9.1 makes that understanding a requirement.
Exam cue: on CIA planning questions, understand how the organization manages a risk area before relying on management's information about it.
